articleTitle: Effect of harmonics on power measurement
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The authors review three-phase power (kW) metering and analyze the effects of harmonics on power measurement. It is shown that the harmonic content of the load waveform affects power measurement significantly. It is suggested that it is necessary to be cognizant of harmonics in relationship to kWh and power-factor billing. The application of digital microprocessor technology to power metering permits the measurement of power very precisely. It is possible with sample data techniques to determine true real power or kWh consumed by the power distribution system or resolve poor power factor questions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Estimating busbar temperatures
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: A tutorial on calculating the temperature of naturally and liquid-cooled DC busbars is presented. Estimation of time constants allows the calculations of time-varying bus temperatures, and the determination of span constants is helpful in calculating heat gradients along busbars. Sample calculations are included. Hewlett Packard 41CX calculator programs are given. They provide the steady-state temperatures of a naturally cooled DC bus and that bus's time and span constants. An analysis of a water-cooled bus system is also presented. The methods shown allow the estimation of the steady-state temperature of DC busbars within about 5 degrees C.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Use of functional descriptions in specifying drive systems
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: It is noted that state-of-the-art drives today have greatly improved features and capabilities due to being software-based (microprocessor-controlled). To exemplify this, attention is given to interfacing to hierarchy devices such as programmable controllers, instrument distributed systems, and other microprocessor-based equipment capable of performing many functions other than just controlling drive speeds. These functions can be programmable controller type functions, process maintenance, diagnostics, and so forth. The authors discuss the resulting need for functional descriptions in specifying drive systems, give an outline of a typical functional description, and offer pointers to permit optimization of the drive system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Recommended practice for installation, termination and testing of insulated power cable as used in the petroleum and chemical industry
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The application of IEEE P-576 is discussed, covering maximum pulling tension, sidewall pressure, jamming, minimum bending radius, minimum installation temperatures, splicing, and high-voltage proof testing. It is emphasized that the use of the procedures can provide a significant increase in life expectancy for an insulated cable system. It is suggested that these practices be considered at both the engineering design and the installation phase of any project.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Addressing nuisance tripping of instantaneous trip breakers in high efficiency motor applications
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: In reviewing the motor starting current phenomena of high-efficiency motors and the National Electrical Code requirements for instantaneous circuit breakers, the author has determined that there are conflicts. Nuisance tripping of the instantaneous circuit breakers has become more prevalent with the introduction of high-efficiency motors. To address this situation, the author proposes changes to the National Electrical Code and the addition of new test requirements for the qualification or listing of the coordinated protective combination starters. With this in place, new guidelines for setting the adjustment of instantaneous circuit breakers in high-efficiency motor applications could be established. The author maintains that the new method would be easier for the user to apply, permit higher trip settings, and provide improved coordination protection.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Open and short circuit behavior of induction motors
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: A set of equations is derived to permit calculation of speed change and generated voltage (both magnitude and phase angle) of an individual induction motor under motor open-circuit or short-circuit conditions, using a calculator. The equations for motor coasting are very accurate. The equations for motor ride-through are nonlinear, and the proposed approach provides a viable and conservative solution to this complex problem. The equations derived were verified by computer.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design, commissioning and operational experience of a heat tracing system with extensive electronic monitoring
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The authors describe one of the most extensive heat-tracing monitoring systems ever installed, the Lisburne Facility at Prudhoe Bay, Alaska. Over 400 circuits in a crude oil separation facility are independently and individually monitored. The results of the initial construction commissioning and the first six months of operation are reported. An analysis of cost effectiveness and engineering lessons learned about the operation of electrical heat-tracing systems are examined in detail. The system is considered to be definitely worth the investment because of the increased reliability compared to a heat-tracing system without monitoring.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automation of reciprocating gas engine compressor packages using programmable logic controllers
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: An approach taken to automate gas-engine/compressor skid-mounted packages is described. Design criteria and special considerations relating to the application of programmable logic controllers (PLCs) are discussed. Using typical industry standard specifications along with I/O lists, sequence narratives, and logic diagrams, the PLCs can be programmed to perform the desired operation. The added capabilities of the PLC enhance simulation, checkout, and startup. The presentation is based on experience gained from the installation of three reciprocating engine/compressor packages on remote unmanned platforms in the Gulf of Mexico.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Derating of induction motors due to waveform distortion
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Derating of induction motors due to harmonic distortion is discussed. It is found that a restriction for the second harmonic should be included in the harmonic distortion limits established by IEEE Standard 519-1981 and derating in some cases should be considered for less than 5% harmonic distortion. Drip-proof machines are found to be less affected by harmonic distortion than totally enclosed machines. Efficiency plays a very important role in the degree of derating; less efficient machines would require a higher derating. Smaller machines (less than 5 HP) are affected more by the harmonics than the larger machines.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: SCADA system for US Navy fuel depot second generation
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: It is noted that the installation of a second-generation SCADA (supervisory control and data acquisition) and instrument system presents the opportunity for upgrading equipment, enhancing system programs, and verifying the system adaptability to the vagaries of a different site location. The authors describe the design and implementation of the pollution control equipment (PCE) system at the US Naval fuel depot in Jacksonville, Florida. System and contractual requirements are defined, and quality assurance plans and procedures are described along with a report of the anomalies of the installation, factory acceptance, and operational system tests.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Unsteady and steady flow control on pumping systems
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: It is shown that PI (proportional-integral) algorithms can be used to solve two problems in the operation of large aqueducts to transport water through pressurized closed conduits. The first problem is that of regulating the discharge, instead of throttling it with a valve, saving that part of the energy supplied to the pump that would be dissipated by the valve. The second problem is that of reducing the intensity of pressure transients during the starting and normal stopping of pumps, i.e. protecting the pumping installation by means of the gradual variation of rotational speed. A possible performance criterion for minimizing the overshoot and the settling time in order to obtain the optimal values of the PI constants is presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Emergency shutdown system (for industrial power systems)
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The authors describe a recent application using redundant programmable logic controllers that provides online diagnostic checking of input/output devices, verifies operation response of shutdown logic, reduces the probability of a fail-dangerous condition, and reduces false trips to rare events. They describe the steps taken in developing the system and examine the various self-checking features (digital input and output checking and analog input checking). They also describe the test logic operation. The authors believe that their approach will result in a high level of confidence in industrial power system operability and in lower costs.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Power system phase rotation and polarized protective relays
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Many common protective relays used in the protection of power equipment are sensitive to phase sequence rotation of the utility supply. The authors describe a method for analyzing the relay response to the respective phase rotation and to other possible variables. They treat voltage and current phasors, maximum- and minimum-torque lines of polarized relays, and the possible effect of system power factor. It is demonstrated that phase rotation usually does not affect zero-sequence polarized relays. Attention is given to the following relays: directional power relay, IEEE protective device no. 32; directional VAR relay, IEEE protective device no. 55; directional current phase relay, IEEE protective device no. 67; and directional current ground relay, IEEE protective Device 67N.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Preservation of large motors and generators from weather on offshore platforms
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The author outlines the problems encountered with moisture condensation in the bearing cavities and internal windings of large motors and generators when proper equipment storage procedures are not practised. He discusses the moisture condensation problems associated with the operation and shutdown of large motors and generators due to weather conditions at the location of the offshore platforms. The platforms discussed here are located on the outer continental shelf in the Santa Barbara Channel of the coast of California. Possible solutions to these problems are examined. It is suggested that large motors and generators should be stored in their original shipping containers, preferably in a warehouse with controlled temperature, dust, dew point, shock, and vibration. Motors and generators enclosed with dust covers that are air tight and stored outdoors should be packed with adequate desiccant bags for moisture control. If space heaters are energized, the electrical machines should not be enclosed in sealed dust covers so that moisture can escape. Motors and generators with antifriction bearings and sleeve bearings should be rotated once every month to keep an oil film on the shaft and bearing surfaces. The equipment must then be resealed to keep moisture out.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Rectifier and DC bus systems design for the copper electrowinning industry
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: It is noted that the use of DC rectifiers and DC bus systems for the copper electrowinning industry has become more widespread during the last 10 years due to the refinement of the solvent extraction process, which has made electrowinning one of the most cost-effective methods of producing copper. The author discusses some of the design features of the large DC rectifier systems, the design basis for the DC bus systems, and some of the problems encountered with the operations of the systems. He suggests means to correct these problems on present and future systems.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Analysis of harmonic pollution on power distribution systems
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Lower-order harmonics (180 Hz to 2000 Hz) generated by nonlinear loads, such as uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units, adjustable frequency drives, computers, etc., cause harmonic pollution. This pollution can cause problems within power distribution systems that can range from the malfunction of protective devices to the physical damage of power system components and loads. The authors present ideas on how to design an industrial power system with the sources of harmonics in mind and, using computer analysis, to determine whether a harmonic problem may exist. They provide information that can be used to measure an existing electrical system that exhibits evidence of a harmonic problem. The use of tools such as commercial harmonic analysis programs and the IEEE standards is suggested to simplify the analysis of systems and provide guidelines that indicate where problems may lie.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automated engineering and design using personal computers
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The authors present an overview of certain CAD (computer-aided design) and CAE (computer-aided engineering) programs and the software application packages developed for use within Fluor Daniel, Inc. The application packages are based on point-of-entry data capture and use a relational database to share data for many different applications. Two application packages are discussed. The first, ILG (instrument loop generation), encompasses the full range of instruments, control systems, and associated wiring. It consists of a family of compiled dBASE III programs, and its purpose is to manipulate engineering data. ILG readily accepts changes throughout the design cycle. The second package, the master application software package, is similar to ILG, except that it interfaces directly with AutoCAD and transfers data between drawings and databases. Whereas ILG handles only data related to instrumentation the master application package handles data related to all aspects of the plant.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Design of a 138 kV gas insulated substation for a large industrial cogeneration facility
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The author describes the design of a 138 kV GIS (gas insulated substation) installed as part of a large industrial cogeneration facility. Special design features required to accommodate the GIS are discussed. Particular attention is given to surge protection and differential settlement criteria. It is concluded that effort expended during the design phase to ensure coordination among the suppliers of the GIS, generator step-up transformer, and 138 kV cable paid off during the installation phase. Installation of the GIS was completed on schedule, and interfacing to the cable and the transformer went smoothly.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: PC-based diagnostic tool for predictive maintenance of equipment in the petroleum and chemical industries
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The authors describe a PC-based monitoring system developed for the monitoring of motor drives used in the petroleum and chemical industries. The monitor uses a versatile front-end data acquisition system that can interface to a variety of transducers. It is used to provide information about the condition of motors and other equipment. Information gathered by the signal conditioning and event monitoring system will provide a database of problem trends which are very valuable to the design engineering teams in developing better and more cost-effective machines and systems. The authors describe the hardware and the software used in the monitor and illustrate several of its applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulation of pipeline holiday detection by time domain reflectometry
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: An analytical electrical transmission line model for an isolated buried pipeline is developed. Elements of the transmission line model are derived mathematically using both field and circuit theory methods. Propagation along the coated pipeline in a multi-layer earth is studied analytically and modeled with a computer. Performance of the transmission line is analyzed. It is shown that time domain reflectometry may provide the pipeline operator with an electrical method for monitoring pipeline coating integrity.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Comparison of NEMA and ultra-high slip motors on cyclic loads
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Cyclic loads, such as eccentric pumping units, cause a varying torque on the driver. Determination of the most efficient induction motor for such a load is discussed. Ultra-high-slip motors as well as NEMA design motors are evaluated. Operating costs and investment are compared. The study indicates that: (1) any type of motor will work on a pumping unit; (2) the motor must be carefully sized to provide minimum operating cost; (3) the least expensive operating cost and the smallest investment are for the motors with the least slip; (4) the lower slip motors cause an increase in peak torque on the unit; and (5) an accurate computer model with an easy-to-use program that allows 'what if' options is highly desirable.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A manual/automatic synchronization circuit for a 37.5 MVA steam turbine driven generator
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: A manual/automatic synchronization circuit has been designed for a 37.5 MVA generator with protection for all three critical synchronizing parameters. The circuit uses triply redundant protective levels for both the manual and automatic circuits. The first and second protective levels, consisting of a solid-state automatic synchronizing relay in tandem with a solid-state synchronization check relay, are shared by both circuits. An operator/synchroscope provides the third protective level for the manual circuit, and a microprocessor-based governor provides the third protective level for the automatic circuit. The author reviews the philosophy, design, and operation of this manual/automatic synchronization circuit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Factors affecting lighting fixture operating temperature, fixture life and subsequent suitability for classified areas
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: A history of the development of early explosionproof incandescent and mercury-vapor lamps and integrally ballasted fixtures is given. The classification of areas in petroleum refineries and chemical facilities, which may be exposed to flammable gases, vapors, or dusts, is discussed, and test methods are briefly described. Problems that arose with the advent of coal gasification and new plastic processes, in which simultaneous exposure to hazardous gases and combustible dusts occurred, are examined. Further process in fixture design, resulting in enclosed and gasketed fixtures suitable for a much broader range of hazardous gases, vapors, and dust and for higher ambient temperatures, is summarized. It is emphasized that today's engineer must be familiar with all the variables which affect industrial lighting fixtures' operating temperature and fixture life in order to specify fixtures which will be safe and reliable in process industry environments. Recommendations on assuring maximum safety and reliability are presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulation of protective relay performance under short circuit and transient swing conditions
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: A comparison of the static and dynamic short-circuit calculation procedures has shown that the dynamic procedure, with enhanced machine modeling, produces results which agree well with national standards and minimizes the engineering design effort, with only a small increase in computational overhead. Time overcurrent relay settings and tripping times obtained by a dynamic short-circuit calculation are compared with fault clearing times obtained by modeling the relays using a traditional step-by-step dynamic analysis procedure. These two very different methods of calculation yield results which are in close agreement, reaffirming the validity of the dynamic short-circuit calculation procedure and offering evidence that the practice of basing the setting of time overcurrent relays on fault currents relating to time t=500 ms is well founded. The authors also demonstrate how inclusion of protection setting and transient modeling facilities in power system CAD (computer-aided design) packages offers the opportunity to include automatically and reliably the effect of the protection in any subsequent transient studies of the system. The main benefit is that this can highlight omissions or sensitivities in the protection arrangements.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Data base techniques for analyzing electric power bills
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Oil and gas production and pipeline companies generally process many electric power bills for considerable amounts of money. It is shown that even though each power company has a different method of figuring electricity costs, simple techniques can be devised to identify potential billing payment mistakes, along with areas for operations improvement. With the use of a computer and database software, these techniques reduce the amount of time spent performing this task compared to analyzing each bill one at a time. The author addresses how to implement this system and relates some experiences that proved that this approach could save significant amounts of money and time. In eight months of using a database to analyze electric power bills, $75000 in billing errors and data entry errors were found, and $25000 per year was saved by improving operational procedures. This was accomplished with minimal capital expenditure, time and effort. Power-factor correction required some capital investment but paid out in less than one year.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Bus transfer of AC induction motors, a perspective
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The author attempts to put the problem of bus transfer of induction motors into perspective by presenting, in general terms, the overall concerns and the methods of analysis recently developed. Some results of a study of bus transfer on a 250 hp motor for various reclosure times are shown. The complex electromagnetic transient and the resulting shaft torque transient for various durations of power interruption are illustrated. It is noted that there is no simple method of analysis available for determining the effects on the rotating components of the motor, the couplings, and the driven equipment. There are several general guidelines in use, but care must be applied when determining if they are applicable to the conditions under consideration. The ANSI C50.41 recommendation of using a 1.33 per unit limit for the resultant vectorial volts per hertz as a determining factor appears to reduce the complexities of the decision too much. The NEMA MG1 recommendation to wait until the motor residual voltage decays to 30% to 25% of its initial value may not be practical for critical equipment. It is concluded that when one does not have the time to delay reclosure, the NEMA MG1 recommendation that a detailed analysis be performed is appropriate.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A practical approach to solving large drive harmonic problems at the design stage
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Harmonics associated with large variable-frequency drives or large groups of smaller drives, which can create severe problems for the industrial plant's power distribution system and the utility's power grid, are discussed. The authors address how to eliminate the harmonic problems early in the design phase of a project and show that it is not an insurmountable task. Attention is given to the creation of harmonic specifications, the information required, harmonic reduction options, design check points, and field verifications. It is concluded that through the proper design and design checks a large electric drive can be installed that will create no harmonic problems for an industrial power system. To assure that a particular system will operate properly, it is necessary to understand basically what harmonic problems can result and design around them. A well-designed system requires that the purchaser provides to the vendor not only a complete operational specification but also some key power system information.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Fast bus-transfer techniques for maintaining full plant production
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Residual-voltage and delayed bus-transfer operations often result in severe process upsets or complete loss of plant production. It is noted that fast transfer techniques might solve such problems, but it is questionable whether they can be safely and effectively applied in petroleum and chemical plants. The author attempts to answer this question by reviewing the strengths and weaknesses of all fast and in-phase transfer schemes, including the newly developed fast transfer switch (FtS). IT is shown that high-speed, in-phase, and Beckwith systems may be applicable to special situations in which inertias are high and initiation is by manual or equivalent means. These schemes should be avoided where initiation is by electrical faults unless the fault type and location are predictable and a full transient analysis is performed. The FTS system is seen to be applicable to loads of any inertia, whether initiated by faults or otherwise. Thus, it appears to be well suited to virtually all petroleum and chemical plant applications. Its main drawback at the present time is a lack of industrial experience with it.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Performance characteristics and design criteria for high-speed adjustable speed drivers for large turbomachines
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Gearless-electric-motor adjustable-speed drives can, in many applications, be an attractive alternative to thermodynamic and hydraulic drivers on high-speed centrifugal pumps and compressors in the uppermost power range. The authors discuss electrical and mechanical design criteria for these synchronous motors as well as their limit ratings, provide actual examples of such machines, and highlight typical performance characteristics. A survey of the required auxiliary electrical equipment, identical to that used on low-speed load-commutated inverter (LCI) drives, and economic considerations are included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Flexible shaft versus rigid shaft electric machines for petroleum and chemical plants
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: A background on electric machines is presented covering power/speed rating charts and the history of motors and turbogenerators. Their applications in petroleum and chemical plants are described. Motor construction, speed/power limits, and vibration and balance are discussed. Recent developments and design conflicts are examined. It is noted that the vast majority of electric machines have been produced according to rigid-shaft design criteria, but an increasing number of large high-speed motors that operate at constant speed are designed with flexible shafts. Flexible-shaft motors may not be well suited to adjustable-speed operation because excessive vibration can occur at some operating speeds, barring continuous running. Rigid-shaft motors have the advantage of being less prone to excessive vibration when operated over a wide speed range. Motors larger than 1/4 the largest rating that can be built with a rigid shaft need more engineering coordination than do smaller motors. With proper coordination, rigid-shaft motors operating on resilient mountings can be made insensitive to vibration. Experience with such drives has not shown a need to restrict continuous operation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Flammability and toxicity testing of wire and cable
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: Numerous entities are developing and implementing new testing requirements to measure the flame propagation characteristics of tray cables and the toxic gases generated during combustion of wire and cable. The author provides an overview of the organizations developing the tests, a general description of the test protocols, their current status, and their potential impact on the petroleum and chemical industries. It is suggested that the establishment of new flame testing criteria for tray cables may eliminate some presently permitted cable constructions. Introduction of new materials that are either more flame retardant, produce less smoke, or generate less corrosive or toxic gases will provide opportunities for new constructions and products.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Automated bus transfer controller and synchronous in-phase relay for critical industrial processes
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The techniques and methods for maintaining continuous electrical power to petroleum and chemical facilities from two or more utility feeders by an automated bus transfer logic controller relay system are discussed. The purpose of this relay system is to reduce transients, torsional forces, inrush currents, and motor stress while maintaining continuous motor operation when the primary facility transfers the motor load to an alternative source of electrical supply. The relay system performs the necessary logic for power-supply bus transfers in two directions by automatically selecting from either the fast, in-phase, or residual voltage methods. The controller continuously monitors the alternative source, the load bus, and the normal source. The economic considerations of maintaining continuity of production during power-supply interruptions using a transfer logic controller to supervise bus transfers may be significant. The engineering studies, application considerations, motor control design requirements, installation, and operation of the automated bus transfer controller for a chemical facility are discussed, and the present bus transfer methods are reviewed. The effectiveness of these methods for typical buses is discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Data and telecommunication system wiring
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: As a result of the breakup of AT&T, corporations are now responsible for installing their own plant telephone networks and telephone and data systems wiring. The authors describe the effort associated with this task at two locations. At one site, 450000 ft of telephone and data cable were installed. Telephone system procurement, installation, and wiring as well as the wiring for data communication networks are reviewed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Lightning protection for microprocessor based electronic systems
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The authors address the issues of lightning threats, suppressor components, and guidelines for selection and placement of protectors for microprocessor-based electronic systems. It is noted that more than 75% of all field failures of microprocessor-based electronic systems are caused by electrical overstress. The fundamental ingredients of an effective protection scheme, namely, grounding, bonding, shielding, and protective devices, are briefly discussed. Protective devices are then examined in more detail, and key parameters for selecting protectors for a specific application are considered. Protector installation is discussed, and some case histories are presented to illustrate the points made.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A case study of replacing steam turbines with LCI type variable speed drives
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: The authors describe the problems and experiences associated with the installation, startup, and operation of 7000 hp, 1800 r/min and 3600 hp, 6000 r/min synchronous motors using LCI (load commutated inverter) variable-speed controllers. Some of the problems and concerns that were encountered on this project were a result of existing equipment worked with, coupled with the dynamics of the electrical, instrumentation, and process systems. It is concluded that, when planning the application of variable-speed drives, factors such as electrical system disturbances, the impact of harmonics on the existing equipment, training, commissioning, operator acceptance, craft training, and spare parts all need to be taken into consideration. If properly designed and installed, these drive systems provide an economical, reliable, variable-speed package for petrochemical installations including large critical applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Control system selection for a process plant: 'Why a DCS may not be the answer'
publicationTitle: Industrial Applications Society, 36th Annual Petroleum and Chemical Industry Conference
abstract: It is noted that reduced process control budgets and powerful new programmable control systems have forced the design engineer to rethink his approach to process control. Traditional minicomputer-based distributed control systems can no longer be justified on process applications independent of their size. The authors describe a recent project which serves as a good example of this scenario. A combination of a limited control system budget and a highly flexible PLC-based system led to the reevaluation of the previously used approach to automatic process control systems. Alternative control system hierarchies were evaluated, comparing traditional approaches to new PLC based systems. A detailed review of the system selected is included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
